source_text: Adorans autem, fratres dilectissimi, nec illud ignoret, quemadmodum in templo cum pharisaeo publicanus orauerit. non adleuatis in caelum inpudenter oculis nec manibus insolenter erectis, pectus suum pulsans et peccata intus inclusa contestans diuinae misericordiae inplorabat auxilium, et cum sibi pharisaeus placeret, sanctificari hic magis meruit qui sic rogauit, qui spem salutis non in fiducia innocentiae suae posuit, cum innocens nemo sit, sed peccata confessus humiliter orauit, et exaudiuit orantem qui humilibus ignoscit. quae Dominus in euangelio suo ponit et dicit: homines duo ascenderunt in templum adorare, unus pharisaeus et unus publicanus. pharisaeus cum stetisset, talia aput se precabatur: Deus, gratias tibi ago, quia non sum sicut ceteri homines iniusti, raptores, adulteri, quomodo et publicanus iste. ieiuno bis in sabbato, decimas do omnium quaecumque possideo. publicanus autem de longinquo stabat et neque oculos suos leuabat ad caelum sed percutiebat pectus suum dicens: Deus, propitius esto mihi peccatori. dico uobis, descendit hic iustificatus in domum suam magis quam ille pharisaeus: quia omnis qui se extollit humiliabitur, et qui se humiliat exaltabitur.
thought_title: The publican's humble prayer heard over the Pharisee's pride
orientation: Cyprian is addressing his beloved brothers, teaching from the Gospel how one ought to pray by contrasting the Pharisee and the publican in the temple.
pass_a_gloss: But when he worships, most beloved brothers, he should not be ignorant of that, in what manner the publican prayed in the temple with the Pharisee. Not with eyes shamelessly lifted up to heaven nor with hands insolently raised, striking his breast and bearing witness to the sins shut up within, he was imploring the help of the divine mercy, and while the Pharisee was pleasing to himself, this man deserved rather to be made holy who prayed in this way, who placed the hope of salvation not in confidence in his own innocence, since no one is innocent, but confessed his sins and prayed humbly, and he who forgives the humble heard the one praying. Which things the Lord sets down in his Gospel and says: two men went up into the temple to worship, one a Pharisee and one a publican. The Pharisee, when he had stood, was praying such things by himself: God, I give thanks to you, because I am not like the rest of men, unjust, robbers, adulterers, just as also this publican. I fast twice in the sabbath, I give tithes of all things whatever I possess. But the publican was standing far off and was not even lifting his eyes to heaven but was striking his breast saying: God, be merciful to me, a sinner. I say to you, this man went down to his house justified rather than that Pharisee: because everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and he who humbles himself will be exalted.

choices.why: The passive infinitive keeps the force that the publican received sanctification rather than achieving it himself; 'hallowed' is reserved for the petition in the Lord's Prayer.

choices.english: bearing witness to the sins shut up within
choices.why: Keeps the legal force of contestans as a public declaration and the image of sins enclosed inside the breast.

choices.english: while the Pharisee was pleasing to himself
choices.why: Preserves the reflexive dative and the imperfect tense, showing the Pharisee's self-satisfaction as the background against which the publican's humility stands out.

choices.english: be merciful to me, a sinner
choices.why: The future imperative esto is rendered as a direct plea; 'propitius' is kept as 'merciful' to match the publican's humble request for divine mercy.
rejected: have mercy on me, a sinner
be gracious to me, a sinner

choices.term: descendit hic iustificatus in domum suam
choices.english: this man went down to his house justified
choices.why: Keeps the perfect passive participle iustificatus as a state resulting from God's action, and the demonstrative hic as emphatic contrast with the Pharisee.
rejected: he went down justified to his house

pass_b_english: But when he worships, dearest brothers, let him not be ignorant of how the publican prayed in the temple with the Pharisee. He did not lift his eyes shamelessly to heaven or raise his hands insolently. He was striking his breast and bearing witness to the sins shut up within, and he was imploring the help of divine mercy. And while the Pharisee was pleasing to himself, this man who prayed in this way deserved more to be made holy, because he did not place his hope of salvation in confidence in his own innocence—since no one is innocent—but confessed his sins and prayed humbly. And the one who forgives the humble heard him as he prayed. The Lord sets this down in his Gospel and says: “Two men went up to the temple to worship, one a Pharisee and one a publican. The Pharisee stood and was praying these things to himself: ‘God, I thank you that I am not like other men—unjust, robbers, adulterers—or even like this publican. I fast twice in the week; I give tithes of everything I possess.’ But the publican stood far off and would not even lift his eyes to heaven, but was striking his breast, saying: ‘God, be merciful to me, a sinner.’ I tell you, this man went down to his house justified rather than that Pharisee. For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and the one who humbles himself will be exalted” (Luke 18:10-14).

last_rejected.quote: deserved more to be made holy
last_rejected.why: "sanctificari" means to be justified/declared righteous, not "made holy" in context; this is the key theological term in the parable.
last_rejected.fix: this man who prayed in this way was rather justified
last_rejected.ruling: sanctificari standardly means 'made holy/sanctified'; justified is iustificatur below. Within normal range, not a major error.

last_rejected.why: "apud se" means "within himself/in his heart" or "privately," not "to himself" as recipient; the Pharisee is not praying to himself.
last_rejected.fix: was praying such things within himself
last_rejected.ruling: aput se precabatur can mean 'prayed to himself'; common rendering of Luke's idiom. Not a major meaning change.
